headline: With six times more data from three sources, ByT5 reaches 3.5% character error
lede: Trained on the original 2,934 Manglish sentences, mBART-50 and ByT5-base reach 6 to 8% character error and cannot be told apart across five seeds. Trained on 18,548 sentences from three datasets (SeLLaI Manglish, SeLLaI Mixed-Code and Dakshina romanised Wikipedia) and scored on 2,059 held-out sentences from all three, ByT5 reaches 3.5%, mBART-50 6.0%, mT5 6.4% (10.0% at the specified learning rate). A rule-based cleaner scores 11.0% and copying the input 21.6%. Overall on the combined test, the models trained on little data (CER 14.8 to 26.8) do worse than that rule-based cleaner.
resultsSub: Original 325-sentence validation set. Mean ± SD over training seeds: five for mBART-50 and ByT5-base, three for mT5 at LR 1e-3, one for mT5 at LR 2e-4 and for every “+ data” row (trained on 18,548 sentences, seed 42). Bold marks the best mean in each column.
dataSub: Each extra source goes through a sanitiser that repairs what it can (Unicode forms, HTML entities, control and zero-width characters, emoji, URLs, repeated punctuation) and drops what it cannot (non-Latin script, truncated fragments, elongated letters, number-heavy or symbol-heavy lines, gibberish, single words). Over-long lines are split at clause boundaries. 10% of every source is held out for the combined test set, which also contains the original 325 validation sentences, and no test sentence appears in any training file. The original Manglish class is audited but not re-filtered, so earlier results stay comparable.
combSub: CER on 2,059 held-out sentences, overall and by source; the bar in each cell is scaled to the largest value. Models trained only on the 2,934 Manglish sentences are poor away from that source: overall they score worse than the rule-based cleaner that only collapses repeated letters, on Dakshina every one of them is worse, and mT5 is worse than copying the input. Only ByT5 on Mixed-Code (10.0 against 11.2) and every model on the Manglish source itself beat the rule-based cleaner. Training on all three sources fixes this.
pairSub: Paired bootstrap over test sentences: CER of the first system minus the second, with a 95% interval. On the small validation set the interval for mBART against ByT5 includes zero, and across five seeds Welch's t is about 1.8 with roughly 4 degrees of freedom, where about 2.8 is needed, so the small-data comparison stays open. On the 2,059-sentence combined test, ByT5 + data beats mBART-50 + data by 2.4 CER points (interval 2.2 to 2.7). That comparison is one training seed per model.
robSub: CER on a fixed 600-sentence subsample of the combined test, with noise the models never saw in training: 2 and 3 times the training rates, vowel dropping and phonetic spelling variants. Models with more data stay far below copying the input and the rule-based cleaner under heavier noise of the trained kind. No model beats copying the input when vowels are dropped. ByT5 + data is best at the trained noise level and at vowel dropping; mBART-50 + data is better at 3 times the noise and with phonetic spellings, so the claim that ByT5 is simply more robust to noise does not hold.
decSub: CER on the same 600 sentences, with greedy decoding or 4-beam search, each with and without a length guard that swaps in the rule-based cleaning when an output is under 60% of the input length. For ByT5 trained on little data the guard replaced about 65 of 600 outputs and cut CER from 16.5 to 10.0. With the larger training set no output needed replacing, and beam search is slightly worse for ByT5 but helps mBART-50 and mT5.
reco:
With enough data, use ByT5-base. Trained on 18,548 sentences it has the lowest error on every source (CER 2.4 on Manglish, 2.2 on Mixed-Code, 4.7 on Dakshina), never needed the length guard, and used less GPU memory than mBART-50 (3.2 GB against 4.2 GB at training peak). The gap to mBART-50 is large on 2,059 test sentences, but it comes from a single training seed, and ByT5's results varied far more between seeds than mBART-50's when data was small (SD 1.6 against 0.2).

Choose mBART-50 for heavier or differently spelled noise. It degrades more gently at 3 times the noise and with phonetic spellings, and it is steadier across seeds.

With only a few thousand sentences, none of the three is a safe choice away from the training source. On the combined test they lose to a rule-based cleaner. If you must, use ByT5 with beam search and the length guard (CER 8.6 against 11.2 for the rule-based cleaner on the 600-sentence subsample).

mT5-base needs both more data and a higher learning rate. At the specified rate it fails on 2,934 sentences and just edges the rule-based cleaner on 18,548; at 1e-3 it edges mBART-50 on Dakshina (CER 7.4 against 7.9) but trails it on the other two sources.
limits: Noise is synthetic: repetition (10% per character) and duplication or deletion (4%). Results show robustness to that noise and to the two extra noise types tested, not to real social-media writing.
The models trained on the combined data ran once (seed 42), so their ranking rests on a large test set but not on seed-to-seed variation. The small-data models ran five seeds.
Two of the three datasets are caption-style (SeLLaI). Dakshina is formal Wikipedia text romanised by hand, with no English mixing, so it tests transfer to a different register.
The 2,059-sentence test set is much larger than the original 325 but still small per source, and exact or near-exact duplicates only are removed between sets.
The robustness and decoding studies use a 600-sentence subsample to keep runtime manageable.
Denoising only. No translation-quality claim is made.
devs: Dataset: three sources, 18,548 training and 2,059 test sentences (20,607 in all, close to the roughly 15,000 in the proposal), not one dataset. The original run used 3,259 Manglish sentences (2,934 train, 325 validation).
Text type: caption-style plus romanised Wikipedia, not social media.
mT5 and ByT5 train in bf16 instead of FP16, because T5-family models overflow in FP16.
mT5 also ran at learning rate 1e-3 instead of 2e-4, labelled as a deviation. Both rates are reported.

Runs on the larger data use the largest micro-batch that fits in GPU memory (2 by 8 for mBART-50, 4 by 4 for ByT5, 8 by 2 for mT5); the effective batch stays at 16 and the other settings are unchanged.
Seeds 43 to 46 were added beyond the proposal's single run, and a second evaluation protocol (the combined test set) beyond the proposal's single validation split.
Noise rates 0.10 and 0.04, a 120-character cap, the mT5 prefix and mBART language code en_XX are choices the proposal leaves open.
